messages.subject: triple interaction random effects
parts:
Dear all,

I want to model a age-space-time interaction term. So far I started implementing the model similar to the code from the paper "Age–space–time CAR models in Bayesian disease mapping" by Goicoa et. al. (DOI: 10.1002/sim.6873). In there they start with indexing over province and age, province and year, age and year. Now I am curious if I can also do the indexing for year province and age. However, I am super uncertain how to do this. 

Can you maybe help me please?

Best,
Corinna

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] triple interaction random effects
parts:
If you know how this age-space-time interaction term is defined, you can do
this. INLA use a one-dimensional indexing, so you only need to define a mapping
from

(age,space,time) -> index

which is unique and invertible. usually, age=1...N.age, space=1...N.space,
time=1...N.time, then one mapping is

index = age + (space-1) * N.age + (time-1) * N.age * N.space

Hi Håvard , maybe this is a stupid response now ( sorry in case ), but I do not really understand how this can be a proper index for space-time-age since 
seq(1,  age + (space-1) * N.age + (time-1) * N.age * N.space) corresponds to 1,2,3,4...., (end of dataframe).

I have age=1,...,20 and space=1,2,..9 and time=1,...100.

I thought I have to build it similar to 
  • Id.prov.year= rep(seq(1, space*time), each=age), which corresponds to 1,.....,180 and then it repeats 20 times
  •  or Id. prov.age= rep(seq(1, space*age), time), which is 1,.....,1 (20 times) and then moves on to 2,.....,2 (20 times) and so on
  •  or Id.year.age=as.vector(apply(matrix(seq(1, age*time), age,time),2, function(x) rep(x, space))), which 1,....20 for the same time and for the next time its 21,...40 and so on
Am I wrong or does Id.space.time.age really correspond to 1,2,3.....(end of dataframe) without any repetition, as you mentioned?

Looking forward to your answer.

Best,
Corinna

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] triple interaction random effects
parts:
you can check like this

N.age <- 3
N.space <- 4
N.time <- 5
for(time in 1:N.time) {
for(space in 1:N.space) {
for(age in 1:N.age) {
idx = age + (space-1) * N.age + (time-1) * N.age * N.space
cat("time=", time, "space=", space, "age=", age, "idx=", idx, "\n")
}
}
}


you can have same 'idx' observered several times, that is no problem.

if your 'age' is not 1:3, as above, you need to map your age, into 1:3
